findings.title: Remark 'a weight that did not work': the 4.178 obstruction is an artifact of starting the a-grid at L+0.01; admissible a near 1.037 gives 4.1463, below the scaling bound
findings.location: Remark [a weight that did not work], paper/main.tex:770-786 (section file lines 182-198)
findings.quote: weight cannot give less than $4.178$, which is worse than the $4.1515$ from
findings.claim: With psi_m=(beta/n)(a-S_A+n t_m), exact fiber evaluation over t'=(x,...,x,0,...,0) shows this weight cannot give less than 4.178 at (k,eps)=(50,1/25), worse than scaling 4.1515; the binding fiber has a single nonzero coordinate x ~ 2 eps; the earlier draft's 4.146 is superseded.
findings.issue: The computation only scans a in np.arange(L+0.01, 3.0, 0.01) = [1.05, 2.99], and the reported optimum (best a=1.05) sits at the lower end of that grid. The weight is positive for every a > tau: for an active index t_m >= S - tau, so a - S_A + n t_m >= a - tau > 0. So a in (0.96, 1.05) is admissible and was never examined. Running the same exact fiber code (dual_eps.fiber_integral, same fiber family) gives a lower bound of 4.15019 at a=1.040 (=L), 4.1469 at 1.036, 4.14633 at 1.037, 4.14651 at 1.038, 4.1478 at 1.039, and 4.1640 at 1.045. With 4000 x-samples per r the value is 4.146328 at a=1.037, binding fiber r=10, x~0.080. So the true obstruction from this test is about 4.146, which is below the scaling 4.1515. The statement 'cannot give less than 4.178', the conclusion 'worse than ... scaling', the explanation that the binding fiber has a single nonzero coordinate (true only for a >= ~1.045), and the parenthetical that the exact evaluation 'supersedes' the earlier 4.146 from 'about ten non-zero coordinates' do not follow. The v0.3 number is in fact reproduced at a ~ 1.037 with r = 9-10. Since the test gives only a lower bound, whether this weight beats scaling is undetermined.
findings.evidence: code/dual_eps.py lines 63-67: 'for a in np.arange(L + 0.01, 3.0, 0.01)'. Rerun of 'dual_eps.py remark16' prints 'bound >= 4.1782 for every a on the grid (best a=1.05; binding fiber r=1, x=0.0820)'. Probe script (scratchpad r16a.py/r16b.py/r16c.py) imports the same fiber_integral; outputs listed above. log/research-log.md Session 3: 'Remark 16 did not reproduce as drafted: exact fiber evaluation gives 4.178 ... not 4.146.'
findings.analysis: This is a lower bound for what the weight certifies (sup over a subfamily of fibers), minimised over a. Restricting a to [1.05,3] is not stated as a hypothesis of the weight, and positivity holds for every a > tau, so the minimum over admissible a is at most 4.1463. Secondary locator: paper/main.tex:785 'about ten non-zero coordinates; the exact fiber evaluation above supersedes it.'
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the a-scan to the full admissible range a > tau (at least [tau+0.001, 3]) and report the minimum (about 4.146 at a ~ 1.037 for these fibers). Withdraw 'worse than the 4.1515 from scaling' and the single-coordinate explanation, or replace them with a full sup over fibers at the optimal a. Restore the v0.3 number, or explain the difference, in the parenthetical. Update log/research-log.md accordingly.

findings.title: prop:family discretisation is neither a restriction nor a relaxation, yet the prose draws a floor for the whole family W at (50,1/25)
findings.location: Text after Proposition prop:family, paper/main.tex:820-822; also 'it tells us how far any weight in $\mathcal W$, however clever, can go', paper/main.tex:795-796
findings.quote: $t_m$ and $S$ can bring the dual bound much below $4.14$ there, while the true
findings.claim: Since B_N(50,1/25) settles near 4.14 (4.1427, 4.1420, 4.1418), no weight of the form Psi(S-t_m,t_m) can bring the dual bound much below 4.14.
findings.issue: B_N restricts Psi to rho*(L-sigma+(k-1)u) with rho piecewise constant on cells, which raises the optimum. It imposes the fiber conditions only at grid sigma and the pointwise condition only at grid configurations, which lowers it. So B_N bounds inf over W in neither direction, as code/dual_lp.py itself says ('not a rigorous bound in either direction'). The paper's own (30,1/4) row shows the upward bias is not small: B_160 = 4.0240 exceeds the value 4.0021 of a known member of W (the two-zone weight) by 0.022. Stabilisation of B_N over N=80..160 shows convergence of the discretised problem, not proximity to inf over W. The cell-wise form cannot represent the two-zone weight exactly; the research log says 'piecewise-constant weights in (sigma,u) could not represent the two-zone weight'. So the bolded lesson that a weight must see more of t than t_m and S, at (50,1/25), is supported only heuristically.
findings.evidence: runs/dual_lp_conv.log: 'k=30 eps=1/4 Nc=160 N=160: LP 4.0240'; two-zone value at (30,1/4) recomputed as 4.002087 (dual_eps_cert.choose). code/dual_lp.py docstring: 'NUMERICAL ONLY: discretised in t, not a rigorous bound in either direction.'
findings.analysis: The proposition header is labelled 'not a rigorous bound', but the prose after it states an unconditional conclusion about all of W. The only control case where the answer is known (eps=0) is degenerate: the classical weight is exactly of the discretised shape with constant rho. The other control case, (30,1/4), shows the bias. Not filed as a demonstrated error because B_N(50,1/25) does lie below the two-zone 4.1458.
findings.suggested_fix: Phrase the conclusion as 'the discretised optimum settles near 4.14; this suggests ...', and note that at (30,1/4) B_N overshoots a known member of W by at least 0.022. Alternatively, add a convergence argument or a genuine relaxation (pointwise constraints on all configurations, e.g. by a Lipschitz margin) that gives a lower bound on inf over W.

findings.title: 'Exact convex solver' is a floating-point interior-point solver that warned 'Solution may be inaccurate' on the reported runs
findings.quote: exact convex solver at each step, is:
findings.claim: B_N is computed by cutting planes with an exact convex solver at each step.
findings.issue: code/dual_lp.py solves each inner problem with cvxpy/CLARABEL, a floating-point interior-point solver, not an exact one. runs/dual_lp_conv.log records 'UserWarning: Solution may be inaccurate' for the k=30 eps=1/4 N=120 and N=160 runs and the k=50 eps=1/25 N=160 run, which are table entries. The values are labelled floating point, so no claim changes, but 'exact' misdescribes the method.
findings.evidence: code/dual_lp.py line ~111 'prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)'; runs/dual_lp_conv.log warning lines interleaved with the RESULT lines.
findings.analysis: Accuracy warnings do not invalidate a value labelled floating point, but they bear on the third-to-fourth digit comparisons (4.1420 vs 4.1418) used to say the values have 'settled'.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'exact convex solver' with 'a floating-point conic solver (Clarabel)', and mention the accuracy warnings, or rerun with tighter tolerances or another solver and record the agreement.

findings.title: Two prop:family table values are not in the cited run logs
findings.location: Table in Proposition prop:family, paper/main.tex:810-811; provenance sentence paper/main.tex:841-843
findings.claim: runs/dual_lp_conv.log and runs/dual_lp_floor.log hold the output.
findings.issue: Every other B_N entry matches the logs: (50,1/25) N=120 4.1420 and N=160 4.1418; (30,1/4) N=80 4.0501, N=120 4.0345 and N=160 4.0240; k=31,32 range 4.0261-4.0976. But the N=80 value 4.1427 at (50,1/25) and the (50,0) N=80 value 3.9919 appear in neither log, nor anywhere else in runs/, log/ or notes/. The same holds for the claim 'the solver, started anywhere, returns k/(k-1) log k' at eps=0. The values could not be regenerated here because cvxpy is not installed.
findings.evidence: grep for '4.1427' and '3.9919' across runs/, log/, notes/ found no match outside the paper; runs/dual_lp_conv.log contains only N=120 and N=160 RESULT lines.
findings.analysis: Provenance gap only; 3.9919 equals 50/49 log 50 = 3.99186, so that entry is plausible.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the N=80 runs at (50,1/25) and (50,0) to runs/dual_lp_conv.log (or a new log), or drop those cells.
